questions.stem: A 67 year old man has a 2 year history of right groin pain that comes on after walking and eases with rest. He is stiff for 10 minutes on waking. Internal rotation of the right hip is reduced and painful. His temperature is 36.7°C, pulse rate 72 bpm and BP 138/82 mmHg. CRP is normal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Mechanical groin pain with short morning stiffness and restricted internal rotation over age 50 is hip osteoarthritis; PMR and RA cause long stiffness and raised CRP.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely diagnosis? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: comes on after walking and eases with rest
Internal rotation of the right hip is reduced
steps.x: **Activity-related** groin pain, **short** morning stiffness, lost internal rotation, normal CRP in an older man.

elim: Lateral hip pain with tenderness over the trochanter; rotation is preserved.
Buttock and leg pain on walking relieved by bending forward; hip movement is normal.
Bilateral shoulder and hip girdle stiffness over an hour, with raised inflammatory markers.
Inflammatory polyarthritis with prolonged morning stiffness and raised CRP.

steps.x: **C. Osteoarthritis of the hip.** Over 50 + activity pain + stiffness under 30 minutes = osteoarthritis.

questions.stem: A 70 year old woman with osteoarthritis of both knees says her fingers have become knobbly and ache after knitting. Morning stiffness in her hands lasts 10 minutes. Her temperature is 36.6°C, pulse rate 76 bpm and BP 140/80 mmHg. Her CRP is normal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on examination of her hands?
o: Bony swellings of the proximal interphalangeal joints
Soft, boggy swelling of the MCP joints
Swan neck deformity of the fingers
Ulnar deviation at the MCP joints
questions.e: Bouchard's nodes are bony swellings of the PIP joints in hand osteoarthritis; MCP synovitis, ulnar deviation and swan necks are rheumatoid.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely finding on examination of her hands? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: Morning stiffness in her hands lasts 10 minutes
steps.x: Hand OA gives **hard bony** nodes: **Bouchard's** at the PIP joints and Heberden's at the DIP joints.

elim: Psoriatic arthritis.
Inflammatory synovitis of rheumatoid arthritis.
Rheumatoid arthritis.
Rheumatoid arthritis.

steps.x: **A. Bony swellings of the proximal interphalangeal joints.** OA hands: Heberden's (DIP) and Bouchard's (PIP). Bony, not boggy.

questions.stem: A 62 year old woman has a 3 year history of aching hands, worse after housework. Morning stiffness lasts 15 minutes. Her temperature is 36.8°C, pulse rate 70 bpm and BP 132/80 mmHg. The doctor is deciding between osteoarthritis and rheumatoid arthritis.
questions.q: Which pattern of joint involvement most supports osteoarthritis?
o: Bilateral wrists and MCP joints affected
Distal interphalangeal joints affected, MCP joints spared
MCP joints of the index and middle fingers only
Symmetrical MCP and PIP joints with DIP sparing
questions.e: Hand osteoarthritis involves the DIP and PIP joints, whereas rheumatoid arthritis spares the DIP joints and affects MCP joints and wrists.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which pattern of joint involvement most supports osteoarthritis? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
OA involves **DIP and PIP** joints. RA **spares the DIPs** and favours MCPs and wrists.

elim: Typical of rheumatoid arthritis.
Suggests haemochromatosis arthropathy.
Typical of gout.
Rheumatoid arthritis spares the DIP joints.

steps.x: **B. Distal interphalangeal joints affected, MCP joints spared.** DIP involvement = OA. DIP sparing = RA.

questions.stem: A 73 year old man has a 5 year history of pain on the inner side of both knees on walking. His trousers have become hard to fit because his legs have changed shape. His temperature is 36.7°C, pulse rate 68 bpm and BP 144/86 mmHg. He has crepitus in both knees.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on examination?
questions.e: Osteoarthritis commonly affects the medial compartment, producing a varus (bow-legged) knee deformity; valgus can occur with lateral disease.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely finding on examination? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
**Medial compartment** OA wears the inner knee first, so the legs bow: a **varus** deformity.

elim: Points to crystal or septic arthritis, not osteoarthritis.
Anterior cruciate ligament rupture.
Chronic tophaceous gout.
Inflammatory arthritis such as rheumatoid.

steps.x: **D. Varus deformity of both knees.** Medial knee OA = varus deformity.

questions.stem: A 41 year old woman has a 2 year history of pain in her left knee on climbing stairs, with intermittent swelling. Her right knee is normal. She had a tibial plateau fracture of the left knee fixed 12 years ago. Her temperature is 36.9°C, pulse rate 74 bpm and BP 122/78 mmHg. CRP is normal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Unilateral osteoarthritis in a younger patient usually follows a previous joint insult such as an intra-articular fracture or ligament or meniscal injury.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely diagnosis? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: tibial plateau fracture of the left knee fixed 12 years ago
steps.x: **Unilateral** OA in a **younger** patient usually follows a previous joint insult such as a **fracture**.

elim: Anterior knee pain in teenagers and young adults without previous fracture.
Sudden, exquisitely painful attacks rather than gradual pain.
Follows infection, with an acute inflammatory joint.
Symmetrical small-joint polyarthritis with raised CRP.

steps.x: **C. Post-traumatic osteoarthritis.** Young + one joint + old injury = secondary (post-traumatic) OA.

questions.stem: A 58 year old woman has pain in both knees on walking. Her BMI is 38. She drinks 6 units of alcohol a week, has never smoked and has a normal diet. Her temperature is 36.8°C, pulse rate 80 bpm and BP 146/90 mmHg. X-ray shows loss of joint space and osteophytes in both knees.
questions.q: Which is the most important modifiable risk factor for her condition?
questions.e: Obesity is one of the strongest risk factors for knee osteoarthritis and is modifiable; weight loss reduces pain.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most important modifiable risk factor for her condition? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Bilateral **weight-bearing** OA with a **BMI of 38**: obesity is one of the strongest risk factors.

elim: Linked to gout, not to osteoarthritis; her intake is low.
A gout risk factor.
Relates to osteoporosis.
She has never smoked and it is not a major OA risk factor.

steps.x: **D. Obesity.** Knee OA risk factor to target = obesity.

questions.stem: A 66 year old woman has osteoarthritis of her hands. For 2 months her right ring finger has clicked and stuck in a bent position in the morning, and she must straighten it with her other hand. There is a tender nodule at the base of the finger in the palm. Her temperature is 36.7°C and pulse rate 72 bpm.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of her finger symptoms?
questions.e: Stenosing tenosynovitis (trigger finger) causes clicking and locking with a palpable nodule at the A1 pulley and may accompany osteoarthritis.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely cause of her finger symptoms? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: clicked and stuck in a bent position
tender nodule at the base of the finger in the palm
steps.x: Clicking and locking with a palmar nodule = **trigger finger**, a stenosing tenosynovitis that can accompany OA.

elim: A fixed, painless flexion contracture from palmar fascia thickening, without clicking.
A smooth swelling, usually on the wrist, that does not lock the finger.
Bony DIP swelling that does not cause triggering.
Causes clawing with weakness and numbness, not clicking.

steps.x: **D. Stenosing tenosynovitis.** Locking finger with a palmar nodule = stenosing tenosynovitis.

questions.stem: A 69 year old man has a 1 year history of a swollen right knee that aches after gardening. He walks with a limp. The knee is cool with a moderate effusion, crepitus and slightly reduced flexion. His temperature is 36.8°C, pulse rate 74 bpm and BP 136/80 mmHg. CRP and ESR are normal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Osteoarthritis can cause an effusion and crepitus with slight restriction, but without fever, erythema or raised inflammatory markers.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely diagnosis? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: knee is cool with a moderate effusion, crepitus
steps.x: Effusion, crepitus, antalgic gait and mild restriction **without** heat, fever or raised markers.

elim: Acute attacks of a hot, exquisitely tender joint.
Acute hot knee attacks, not a chronic cool effusion.
Polyarticular and inflammatory with raised CRP and ESR.
Acute, hot joint with fever and raised CRP.

steps.x: **B. Osteoarthritis.** Cool effusion + crepitus + normal CRP = OA.

questions.stem: A 66 year old man has a 3 year history of pain in both knees, worse at the end of the day. Morning stiffness lasts 15 minutes. He has no fever or weight loss. His temperature is 36.6°C, pulse rate 70 bpm and BP 134/84 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on examination of his knees?
o: Hot, red skin over the joint
questions.e: Crepitus on palpation of a moving joint is typical of osteoarthritis; heat, redness and boggy synovitis suggest an inflammatory or septic process.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely finding on examination of his knees? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: worse at the end of the day
steps.x: Bilateral activity-related knee pain with short stiffness = OA. Rough cartilage surfaces give **crepitus**.

elim: Points to septic or crystal arthritis.
Anterior cruciate ligament rupture.
Not a feature of OA; tophi or rheumatoid nodules occur on extensor surfaces.
Inflammatory synovitis of rheumatoid arthritis.

steps.x: **A. Crepitus on movement.** OA knee on examination: crepitus, effusion, slight restriction, no heat.

questions.stem: A 78 year old woman had a total hip replacement for osteoarthritis 12 years ago. Over 6 months she has had increasing pain in the right groin and thigh on standing and walking. She has no fever. Her temperature is 36.8°C, pulse rate 74 bpm and BP 136/80 mmHg. CRP is normal. X-ray shows a lucent line around the femoral stem.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Aseptic loosening is the most common reason for hip revision, causing gradual weight-bearing pain with lucency around the implant and normal inflammatory markers.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely diagnosis? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: increasing pain in the right groin and thigh on standing
lucent line around the femoral stem
steps.x: Gradual pain years after a hip replacement, normal CRP, **lucency around the stem** = loosening without infection.

elim: Follows a fall with sudden pain and a visible fracture line.
Possible, but she has no fever and CRP is normal.
Sudden 'clunk' with a shortened, internally rotated leg.
Lateral hip tenderness, without a lucent line around the stem.

steps.x: **A. Aseptic loosening.** Commonest cause of hip revision = aseptic loosening.

questions.stem: A 71 year old man had a total knee replacement for severe osteoarthritis yesterday. Today he cannot lift his left foot and it slaps on the floor when he walks. There is numbness over the top of the foot. His temperature is 37.0°C, pulse rate 82 bpm and BP 130/78 mmHg.
questions.q: Which nerve is most likely to have been injured?
questions.e: The common peroneal nerve is the nerve most at risk in knee arthroplasty and causes foot drop with numbness over the dorsum of the foot.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which nerve is most likely to have been injured? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: numbness over the top of the foot
steps.x: Foot drop with numbness of the dorsum after **knee arthroplasty** = **common peroneal nerve**, which winds round the fibular neck.

elim: Weak knee extension and numbness over the front of the thigh.
Weak hip adduction with medial thigh numbness.
Wider weakness of the hamstrings and all muscles below the knee; more at risk in hip surgery.
Weak plantarflexion with numbness of the sole.

steps.x: **A. Common peroneal nerve.** Knee replacement + foot drop = common peroneal nerve.

questions.stem: A 72 year old woman had a total hip replacement for osteoarthritis 3 weeks ago. She felt a sudden clunk and severe hip pain while getting out of a low armchair. She cannot weight-bear. Her temperature is 36.9°C, pulse rate 102 bpm and BP 148/88 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most likely position of her right leg?
questions.e: Posterior dislocation is the classic early complication of hip replacement, with a clunk, leg shortening and internal rotation; external rotation suggests a hip fracture.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely position of her right leg? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: getting out of a low armchair
steps.x: Deep hip flexion after a hip replacement then a **clunk** = **posterior dislocation**: shortened, internally rotated leg.

elim: Not a typical prosthetic dislocation position.
Anterior dislocation is rarer and gives external rotation.
Unlikely after a painful clunk with inability to weight-bear.
The classic position of a fractured neck of femur.

steps.x: **E. Shortened and internally rotated.** Posterior hip dislocation = short and internally rotated.

questions.stem: A 58 year old woman has had pain in her hands and right knee for 2 years, worse after activity. Morning stiffness lasts 10 minutes. She has bony swellings of several DIP joints. Her temperature is 36.7°C, pulse rate 72 bpm and BP 130/78 mmHg. She asks which scan will confirm the diagnosis.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next step to confirm the diagnosis?
o: Plain X-ray of the hands and knee
questions.e: NICE: diagnose osteoarthritis clinically, without imaging, in people over 45 with activity-related joint pain and no or short morning stiffness.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate next step to confirm the diagnosis? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Age **over 45**, activity-related pain and stiffness **under 30 minutes**: NICE says diagnose **clinically**.

elim: Tests for rheumatoid arthritis; the picture is osteoarthritis.
Not needed for a typical presentation.
Only needed if features are atypical or another diagnosis is suspected.
Tests for gout.

steps.x: **B. Diagnose clinically without investigation.** Over 45 + activity pain + stiffness under 30 min = clinical diagnosis.

questions.stem: A 75 year old man has severe right groin pain on walking despite analgesia and is being considered for hip replacement. His temperature is 36.8°C, pulse rate 70 bpm and BP 142/84 mmHg. An X-ray of the pelvis is taken.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on X-ray of the hip?
o: Narrowed joint space with subchondral cysts
Punched-out erosions with a normal joint space
questions.e: Osteoarthritis X-rays show loss of joint space, osteophytes, subchondral cysts and subarticular sclerosis; periarticular osteopenia is rheumatoid.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely finding on X-ray of the hip? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: severe right groin pain on walking
steps.x: OA X-ray: **L**oss of joint space, **O**steophytes, **S**ubchondral cysts, **S**ubarticular sclerosis (LOSS).

elim: Pseudogout.
Rheumatoid arthritis.
Chronic gout.
An effusion or septic joint, not OA.

steps.x: **B. Narrowed joint space with subchondral cysts.** OA X-ray = LOSS.

questions.stem: A 63 year old woman has a 1 year history of pain at the base of her left thumb when gripping pans and pinching. There is tenderness and crepitus at the base of the thumb. Her temperature is 36.6°C, pulse rate 74 bpm and BP 128/76 mmHg. An X-ray of the hand is taken.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on X-ray of the hand?
o: Joint space loss and osteophytes at the first carpometacarpal joint
Soft tissue swelling over the radial styloid only
questions.e: First carpometacarpal osteoarthritis causes pain with gripping and pinching; X-ray shows joint space loss, osteophytes and squaring at the thumb base.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely finding on X-ray of the hand? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: crepitus at the base of the thumb
steps.x: Thumb-base pain on **gripping and pinching** = **first CMC** OA. X-ray shows OA changes with **squaring** of the thumb.

elim: Rheumatoid arthritis.
Follows a fall on the outstretched hand.
Psoriatic arthritis.
De Quervain's tenosynovitis gives tenderness here with a normal X-ray.

steps.x: **C. Joint space loss and osteophytes at the first carpometacarpal joint.** Base of thumb OA = first CMC joint.

questions.stem: A 67 year old woman with knee osteoarthritis has sudden pain behind her left knee, then swelling of the left calf over 6 hours. There is mild bruising around the ankle. Her temperature is 36.9°C, pulse rate 84 bpm and BP 138/80 mmHg. She has no history of venous thrombosis.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?
o: Ultrasound of the popliteal fossa and calf veins
questions.e: A ruptured Baker's cyst mimics a DVT, so ultrasound of the popliteal fossa and calf veins is used to show the cyst and exclude thrombosis.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: sudden pain behind her left knee
steps.x: OA knee + sudden posterior pain + calf swelling and **bruising** = ruptured **Baker's cyst**, which **mimics a DVT**.

elim: She has no chest symptoms.
Not the first test; ultrasound answers the question faster.
Shows OA but not a ruptured cyst or clot.
Invasive and not first-line for leg swelling.

steps.x: **D. Ultrasound of the popliteal fossa and calf veins.** Calf swelling in OA knee: ultrasound to separate Baker's rupture from DVT.

questions.stem: A 72 year old man has a 2 year history of a swollen left knee that aches after walking. The knee is cool with a moderate effusion and crepitus. His temperature is 36.7°C, pulse rate 70 bpm and BP 136/82 mmHg. The knee is aspirated to relieve the swelling.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on synovial fluid analysis?
o: Clear, viscous fluid with a low white cell count
Turbid fluid with a very high neutrophil count
questions.e: Osteoarthritis causes low-grade synovial inflammation from cartilage debris, so aspirated fluid is clear and viscous with a low white cell count.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely finding on synovial fluid analysis? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
OA synovitis is **low-grade**, so the fluid is non-inflammatory: **clear**, viscous, few white cells.

elim: Haemarthrosis after trauma or with anticoagulants.
Gout.
Septic arthritis.
Inflammatory, crystal or septic arthritis.

steps.x: **B. Clear, viscous fluid with a low white cell count.** OA effusion = non-inflammatory fluid.

questions.stem: A 61 year old woman has a 4 year history of aching fingers that is worse after typing. She has hard, non-tender swellings at the distal interphalangeal joints of several fingers. Her nails and skin are normal. Her temperature is 36.6°C, pulse rate 70 bpm and BP 128/78 mmHg. CRP and rheumatoid factor are normal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Heberden's nodes at the DIP joints, with Bouchard's at the PIP joints, are the signature of nodal hand osteoarthritis; psoriatic arthritis needs skin or nail disease.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely diagnosis? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: hard, non-tender swellings at the distal interphalangeal joints
Her nails and skin are normal
steps.x: Hard, bony DIP swellings = **Heberden's nodes**. Normal nails and skin argue against psoriatic arthritis.

elim: Acute hot attacks; tophi are chalky and often over extensor surfaces.
DIP disease with nail pitting and psoriasis, which she does not have.
Spares the DIP joints and causes soft synovitis with raised CRP.
Skin tightening, Raynaud's and calcinosis rather than bony DIP nodes.

steps.x: **B. Nodal osteoarthritis.** Bony DIP nodes, normal nails = nodal OA.

questions.stem: A 77 year old man had a total hip replacement 11 years ago. He has 4 months of gradually increasing right thigh pain on walking. He has no fever and the wound is healed. His temperature is 36.7°C, pulse rate 74 bpm and BP 142/86 mmHg. The surgeon suspects loosening but wants to exclude infection first.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?
o: CRP and X-ray of the hip
Hip aspiration in clinic before any imaging
questions.e: Aseptic loosening is the commonest reason for hip revision; the initial work-up is an X-ray for periprosthetic lucency and CRP to screen for infection.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Late, gradual pain after a hip replacement = **aseptic loosening** until proven otherwise. **CRP** screens for infection and **X-ray** shows lucency.

elim: Not the first test; plain imaging and markers come first.
Not first-line; X-ray shows the lucency.
Comes after bloods and X-ray if infection is still suspected.
Metal artefact limits it; not first-line.

steps.x: **B. CRP and X-ray of the hip.** Painful old hip replacement: X-ray + CRP first.

questions.stem: A 64 year old woman with knee osteoarthritis has taken paracetamol 1 g four times a day for 3 months with little benefit. She has not had physiotherapy and has no other medical problems. Her temperature is 36.8°C, pulse rate 74 bpm and BP 130/80 mmHg. Her eGFR is 82 ml/min/1.73m².
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
o: Stop paracetamol and start topical ibuprofen with physiotherapy
questions.e: First-line treatment for knee osteoarthritis is a topical NSAID with physiotherapy and exercise; routine paracetamol should not be offered.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the next most appropriate step in management? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: paracetamol 1 g four times a day for 3 months
steps.x: NICE: first-line knee OA is a **topical NSAID with exercise/physiotherapy**. Routine **paracetamol is not offered**.

elim: Opioids are not routine for OA and paracetamol should not be offered routinely.
Not recommended by NICE for OA.
Only for severe, refractory disease after core treatments.
Not recommended by NICE.

steps.x: **E. Stop paracetamol and start topical ibuprofen with physiotherapy.** Knee OA first-line = topical NSAID + physio; no routine paracetamol.

questions.stem: A 70 year old man has severe knee osteoarthritis despite topical diclofenac and physiotherapy. He had a myocardial infarction 2 years ago and has type 2 diabetes, hypertension and smokes. His eGFR is 76 ml/min/1.73m². His temperature is 36.7°C, pulse rate 68 bpm and BP 142/84 mmHg. He wants relief for a family holiday next month.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
questions.e: Oral NSAIDs are contraindicated with multiple vascular risk factors; an intra-articular corticosteroid injection gives effective but temporary relief in severe OA.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate management? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: relief for a family holiday next month
steps.x: **Multiple vascular risk factors** rule out oral NSAIDs. An **intra-articular steroid** gives effective but **temporary** relief.

elim: Oral NSAIDs are contraindicated with multiple vascular risk factors.
Still an NSAID, avoided with his cardiovascular risk.
Not appropriate first for OA pain.
Not arranged for a holiday; an injection gives faster short-term relief.

steps.x: **A. Intra-articular methylprednisolone injection.** Severe OA, NSAIDs unsafe, needs quick relief = intra-articular steroid.

questions.stem: A 52 year old man has knee osteoarthritis not helped by topical NSAIDs and physiotherapy. He has no history of indigestion, peptic ulcer or kidney disease and no cardiovascular risk factors. He is started on oral celecoxib. His temperature is 36.6°C, pulse rate 70 bpm and BP 124/78 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate additional prescription?
questions.e: NICE recommends a proton pump inhibitor alongside any oral NSAID, including celecoxib, for all people with osteoarthritis, even without GI history.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate additional prescription? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: no history of indigestion, peptic ulcer
steps.x: NICE: co-prescribe a **PPI** with **any oral NSAID**, including COX-2 inhibitors, in **all** OA patients.

elim: Adds bleeding risk and has no role in OA.
Not required, and constipating.
Should not be routinely offered.
An H2 blocker; NICE recommends a PPI.

steps.x: **C. Omeprazole.** Oral NSAID in OA = always add a PPI.

questions.stem: A 74 year old woman has severe left knee osteoarthritis. She has pain at night and can walk only 50 metres despite topical and oral NSAIDs, physiotherapy, weight loss and two steroid injections. X-ray shows complete loss of medial joint space. Her temperature is 36.8°C, pulse rate 72 bpm and BP 136/82 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate definitive management?
questions.e: Joint arthroplasty is the definitive treatment for severe osteoarthritis that is refractory to non-surgical treatment.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate definitive management? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: complete loss of medial joint space
steps.x: **Severe, refractory** OA with night pain and failed core treatment: **joint arthroplasty**.

elim: Not recommended for OA.
Gives only temporary relief and has already failed.
Not recommended by NICE.
Does not treat the joint and has major side effects.

steps.x: **E. Total knee replacement.** Severe refractory OA = joint replacement.

questions.stem: A 68 year old man on haemodialysis for end-stage kidney disease has severe right knee osteoarthritis. Physiotherapy and weight loss advice have not helped. His temperature is 36.9°C, pulse rate 76 bpm and BP 150/88 mmHg. He is not fit for surgery.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
o: Topical diclofenac to both knees at high dose
questions.e: In kidney disease NSAIDs are avoided; severe osteoarthritis can be treated with an intra-articular steroid injection at a low dose in end-stage renal disease.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate management? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
**Kidney disease** rules out oral NSAIDs. Severe OA: **intra-articular steroid**, at a **low dose** in renal failure.

elim: Oral NSAIDs are contraindicated in kidney disease.
Contraindicated in kidney disease.
Systemic absorption increases at high dose; not the next step.
He is not fit for surgery.

steps.x: **A. Low-dose intra-articular corticosteroid injection.** OA + renal failure: no NSAIDs, low-dose IA steroid.

questions.stem: A 56 year old man has just been diagnosed with knee osteoarthritis. His BMI is 33. He asks what will help his knees most in the long term. He has no other medical problems. His temperature is 36.7°C, pulse rate 74 bpm and BP 134/84 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate long-term management?
questions.e: NICE core treatment for osteoarthritis is exercise with physiotherapy throughout, plus weight loss if overweight, within a multidisciplinary approach.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate long-term management? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Core OA treatment for everyone: **exercise/physiotherapy** throughout, plus **weight loss** if overweight.

elim: Not recommended by NICE.
Not recommended by NICE.
Not recommended by NICE.
Opioids are not a long-term core treatment.

steps.x: **B. Exercise programme and weight loss.** OA core = exercise + weight loss + education.

questions.stem: A 70 year old man had a total hip replacement 4 weeks ago. He felt a clunk while bending to tie his shoelaces and now has a shortened, internally rotated right leg. X-ray confirms a posterior dislocation with no fracture. His temperature is 36.8°C, pulse rate 104 bpm and BP 152/90 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
questions.e: A dislocated hip prosthesis is usually reduced closed under anaesthesia; revision is kept for recurrent or irreducible dislocation.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate initial management? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Acute **posterior dislocation** of a hip replacement without fracture: **closed reduction** under anaesthesia.

elim: The hip will not relocate on its own.
Reserved for recurrent or irreducible dislocation.
Helps prevent recurrence, not treat a current dislocation.
Not the treatment for an acute prosthetic dislocation.

steps.x: **B. Closed reduction under anaesthesia.** Dislocated THR = closed reduction first.

questions.stem: An 80 year old woman had a total hip replacement 14 years ago. She has 9 months of worsening groin and thigh pain on walking. CRP and ESR are normal and hip aspiration is sterile. X-ray shows a wide lucent zone around the femoral stem that has increased since last year. Her temperature is 36.7°C, pulse rate 72 bpm and BP 140/82 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate definitive management?
questions.e: Aseptic loosening is the most common reason for revision hip surgery; a symptomatic loose implant needs revision arthroplasty.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate definitive management? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: wide lucent zone around the femoral stem
steps.x: Progressive lucency with sterile aspirate = **aseptic loosening**, the commonest reason for **revision**.

elim: For dislocation, not loosening.
Does not fix a loose implant.
Aspiration is sterile and markers are normal.
Does not re-fix a loose prosthesis.

steps.x: **E. Revision hip arthroplasty.** Aseptic loosening = revision arthroplasty.

questions.stem: A 63 year old woman has osteoarthritis of both knees. Her student asks what the main disease process is. Her temperature is 36.7°C, pulse rate 72 bpm and BP 132/80 mmHg. CRP is normal and X-ray shows joint space narrowing and osteophytes.
questions.q: Which is the primary pathological process in osteoarthritis?
o: Urate crystal deposition in the joint
questions.e: Osteoarthritis is progressive loss of articular cartilage, from breakdown by matrix metalloproteinases exceeding repair, with osteophytes and synovitis.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the primary pathological process in osteoarthritis? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
OA is **degeneration of cartilage**: breakdown by **matrix metalloproteinases** outpaces repair. Joint space narrows.

elim: Rheumatoid arthritis.
Pseudogout.
Rheumatoid or gouty erosion, not the primary OA process.
Gout.

steps.x: **D. Progressive loss of articular cartilage.** OA = cartilage loss (breakdown beats repair).

questions.stem: A 76 year old man has hip osteoarthritis. X-ray shows the bone just beneath the joint surface is unusually dense and white on both sides of the narrowed joint. His temperature is 36.8°C, pulse rate 70 bpm and BP 138/84 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most likely explanation for the dense bone?
o: Subchondral bone remodelling after cartilage loss
questions.e: As cartilage is lost, subchondral bone remodels in attempted repair, producing subarticular sclerosis and osteophytes.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely explanation for the dense bone? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: dense and white on both sides of the narrowed joint
steps.x: **Subarticular sclerosis**: subchondral bone remodels as cartilage is lost, an attempted repair that also forms osteophytes.

elim: Chondrocalcinosis of pseudogout, seen in the cartilage, not bone.
No fracture is described.
Patchy dense lesions, not a symmetrical band at the joint surface.
Coarse trabeculae and bone enlargement, not limited to the joint margins.

steps.x: **E. Subchondral bone remodelling after cartilage loss.** Sclerosis and osteophytes = bone remodelling (attempted repair).

questions.stem: A 68 year old woman has a swollen left knee from osteoarthritis. The knee is cool, she has no fever and her CRP is normal. Her temperature is 36.6°C, pulse rate 74 bpm and BP 134/78 mmHg. She asks why her knee swells if it is not 'inflammatory arthritis'.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of her knee effusion?
questions.e: In osteoarthritis cartilage debris causes low-grade synovial inflammation, producing an effusion without the systemic response of inflammatory arthritis.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely cause of her knee effusion? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: The knee is cool, she has no fever and her CRP is normal
steps.x: Cartilage debris causes **low-grade synovial inflammation**, enough for an effusion but without a **systemic** response.

elim: Rheumatoid arthritis, with a raised CRP.
Septic arthritis, with fever and a hot joint.
Haemarthrosis, after trauma or anticoagulants.
Gout, with an acutely hot joint.

steps.x: **D. Low-grade synovitis from cartilage debris.** OA effusion = low-grade synovitis, normal CRP.

questions.stem: A 49 year old man with a BMI of 36 has early osteoarthritis of both knees. He also had a meniscal tear of the right knee repaired 10 years ago, and that knee is worse. His temperature is 36.8°C, pulse rate 76 bpm and BP 140/88 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism by which these factors increase his risk?
o: Increased mechanical loading accelerating cartilage wear
questions.e: Obesity and previous joint injury increase osteoarthritis risk because increased or abnormal mechanical loading accelerates cartilage wear.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely mechanism by which these factors increase his risk? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: meniscal tear of the right knee repaired 10 years ago
steps.x: Obesity and an old meniscal injury both raise **mechanical load** on the cartilage, so it **wears faster**.

elim: Not the mechanism of OA.
Linked to obesity but causes gout, not OA.
Osteoporosis; obesity tends to increase bone density.
Septic arthritis.

steps.x: **B. Increased mechanical loading accelerating cartilage wear.** Obesity and old injury = more load = faster cartilage wear.

questions.stem: A 71 year old man with knee osteoarthritis has had a soft swelling behind his right knee for months. Yesterday it disappeared suddenly and his calf became painful and swollen. Ultrasound shows no deep vein thrombosis but fluid tracking into the calf muscles. His temperature is 36.9°C, pulse rate 80 bpm and BP 138/82 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of his calf swelling?
o: Bleeding from a popliteal artery aneurysm
Blood clot in the popliteal vein
Synovial fluid leaking from a ruptured popliteal cyst
questions.e: A Baker's cyst is herniated synovial fluid in the popliteal fossa; rupture releases fluid into the calf, causing pain and swelling that mimic a DVT.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely mechanism of his calf swelling? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: soft swelling behind his right knee
fluid tracking into the calf muscles
steps.x: Baker's cysts form from **synovial fluid herniating** into the popliteal fossa; **rupture** releases fluid into the calf, **mimicking a DVT**.

elim: A pulsatile mass, not fluid from the knee.
Ultrasound excludes a DVT.
Would cause skin redness and fever.
Gives gradual oedema, not sudden pain when the swelling vanishes.

steps.x: **E. Synovial fluid leaking from a ruptured popliteal cyst.** Ruptured Baker's cyst = synovial fluid in the calf, DVT mimic.
